newsitem.title: ZAIRE: 3,000 refugees found in Zaire as aid picks up.
newsitem.headline: 3,000 refugees found in Zaire as aid picks up.

text.p: Aid workers said on Thursday they had found 3,000 Hutu refugees in and near the Zairean town of Ubundu as an operation to help them survive picked up pace.
They said aid workers on Wednesday reached Ubundu, 100 km (60 miles) south of the northeastern city of Kisangani, by train and found 2,510 refugees at km 81 (mile 50) and another 491 in the town.

"There were 491 refugees in Ubundu in a very weakened state including 96 unaccompanied children. They were all in a very bad state. The priority now is to move them to the camps," Paul Stromberg of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said by telephone from Kisangani.
"They reported 141 people had died in Ubundu since March 19 until Tuesday. Residents said that the alliance (rebels) had walked into Ubundu without firing a shot on Sunday," he added.
"Along the way to Ubundu the team left plastic sheeting and soap in an effort to get the local villagers to bury the dead and bring the seriously ill to the railway tracks," he said.

Aid workers said many of the Rwandan and Burundian refugees in Ubundu were living in the open and others had fled into the forest as they were frightened of the Tutsi-dominated Zairean rebels who seized Kisangani last month.
Stromberg said 108 refugees died at two sites for 80,000 south of Kisangani on Thursday from sickness and malnutrition, down from an average of 120 per day last week but still much too high.

U.N. officials said on Tuesday that preparations could take a week to 10 days more before they can start an operation to airlift home the estimated 100,000 refugees south of Kisangani who have fled the Zairean rebels for six months.
UNHCR is still waiting to hear if Rwanda's government would let planes fly from Kisangani to Rwanda. The airlift would be one of the biggest ever mounted and is expected to cost millions of dollars.

Michele Quintaglie, a spokeswoman for the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) in Kisangani, said another team of aid workers investigated how much Zairean villagers had lost to the Hutu refugees in the area to ease tension between the two groups.

"They agreed with each family how to compensate them for what they had lost from their fields. All they are asking for is compensation for what they lost because most of them are subsistence farmers so can't afford a crop," Quintaglie said.
"It sounds small but for instance one family had lost a jerry can but it was the only jerry can they had," she added.
She said the team found that in many villages poor Zairean families had taken in sick and exhausted refugees and fed them.

Major-General Paul Kagame, Rwanda's military strongman and vice president, was quoted by a Belgian newspaper as saying taking back the 100,000 refugees posed no problem but he was sure that some did not want to return to their homeland.
Rwandan authorities will closely screen returnees, the rump of more than two million Hutus who fled into exile in 1994.

Some took part in the genocide of 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates in Rwanda in 1994. Former Rwandan troops and militiamen among them also fought alongside Zairean troops in eastern Zaire against the advancing rebels since last October.
